newsitem.title: THAILAND: Foreign businesses won't leave Cambodia - analysts.
newsitem.headline: Foreign businesses won't leave Cambodia - analysts.

text.p: Violence in Cambodia has jolted the investment climate but Second Prime Minister Hun Sen's steady consolidation of power will restore foreign confidence and stop businesses from pulling out, analysts said on Tuesday.

Analysts said the United States, the European Union and other countries had gone through the routine of condemning Hun Sen's coup but did not expect them to call for an international boycott of the country which would hit its limited exports such as textiles.

Malaysia, the largest foreign investor in Cambodia with $3 billion in projects, last week evacuated hundreds of its citizens employed at various companies in Cambodia but several Malaysian companies said they were not withdrawing from projects.

International Trade and Industry Minister Rafidah Aziz said on Monday Kuala Lumpur would assist Malaysian firms operating in Cambodia to restart their operations once the political situation returned to normal.
"We will try to minimise the dislocation brought about by this disruption," she said.

Thanachai Chintana, managing director of Kongka Knitting Factory Co Ltd, which invested about 10 million baht ($345,000) in a garment factory in a Phnom Penh suburb early this year, said he had no plans to pull out.
"We are already there. The dramatic change of government is a seriously negative development but I think businessmen can eventually adjust to the new environment," he said.
"I don't think the Hun Sen government would do anything drastic as it also needs foreign investment. I don't think many projects will be forced to pull out."
Indonesia's state-controlled PT Indonesian Satellite Corp (Indosat) also said earlier this week that it remained committed to its 49 percent stake in Cambodian telecommunications firm Camintel, S.A.

Alex Sanford of Freshfields, an Indochina investment consultant firm, said Hun Sen's coup had eroded business stability in Cambodia but Phnom Penh could move to reassure foreign investors by calling early elections.

"The change has made things a bit less predictable, less stable. People will sit back on the sidelines, taking a wait-and-see attitude ... I think it would be smart for Hun Sen to announce he would call free and fair elections early, say in six months," Sanford said.
Hun Sen said on Sunday, a week after he ousted First Prime Minister Prince Norodom Ranariddh, that the country must have free and fair elections, but gave no date for the poll.
Sanford said Hun Sen's efforts to gain government legitimacy after ousting Ranariddh had been boosted by the defection of ministers from the deposed prince's FUNCINPEC royalist party.

Eugene Davis of business consulting firm Finansa Thai Ltd. said the end of Cambodia's unstable dual prime minister system could even help restore some stability to the country in the longer run if a clear, single voice emerged on the country's political and economic affairs.
Sanford of Freshfields agreed. "Any time that you have two factions, you've got problems. Factionalism is the danger," he said.
But analysts warned that foreign investor confidence would be further damaged if fighting between forces loyal to Hun Sen and Ranariddh dragged on, or if authorities failed to stop looting in cities.
"The problem is not Hun Sen as an individual. It is the shooting and looting by soldiers that makes people nervous," said Davis of Finansa.
The United States, Germany and Australia have cut or suspended development and military aid to Cambodia to put pressure on Hun Sen to restore constitutional rule and hold early elections.
But Australia decided that general humanitarian and development aid would continue.
Caltex Cambodia Ltd officials said on Tuesday they were delaying plans to expand their retail petrol station business in the country after the recent turmoil there.

But Caltex, the largest U.S. investor in Cambodia, said they would press ahead with plans to complete their largest project, an $8 million international marine terminal in the southern port city of Sihanoukville, by early next year.
